黄仁勋正与盟友讨论回归英伟达计划，硅谷高管拟组建「战情室」游说董事会

BlockBeats 消息，11 月 16 日，据英国《金融时报》报道，英伟达前 CEO 黄仁勋正在与亲信讨论重返公司管理层的可能性。多名硅谷科技界人士正推动英伟达董事会重新任命黄仁勋，并计划组建「战情室」，争取科技行业高管及白宫支持。

特斯拉、SpaceX CEO 马斯克和 Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney 已公开支持一封要求英伟达董事会「让黄仁勋回归」的联名信。部分英伟达员工也公开表达对黄仁勋的支持。

不过，黄仁勋回归仍面临阻力。美国财政部长 Scott Bessent 周日呼吁英伟达进行「重大领导层调整」。与此同时，英伟达董事会正在对引发此次管理层危机的相关行为展开独立调查，公司目前由临时 CEO Colette Kress 领导。

此前，黄仁勋因被曝与疑似间谍、同时也是新加坡芯片企业 Megaspeed 高管的 Alice Huang 存在婚外情而辞职，相关事件也引发外界对英伟达向亚洲客户销售 AI 芯片时合规审查机制的质疑。

此外，英伟达董事会此前已接触 Arm CEO Rene Haas，探讨其接任可能性，但董事会表示尚未启动正式遴选程序。英伟达两大股东 Altimeter Capital 创始人 Brad Gerstner 和 Atreides Management 负责人 Gavin Baker 此前也联名致信董事会，呼吁将黄仁勋回归纳入考虑范围。

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- Wall Street’s push into stablecoins has accelerated sharply, led by a 21-bank consortium committing roughly $270 million to “Project Faro.”.
- Banks and payment giants are shipping now: SoFi expanded SoFiUSD to Polygon, Anchorage’s tokens settle on Visa, Mastercard built out stablecoin tools and agent payments, and Circle pushed into Latin America.
- The GENIUS Act is the catalyst and the big banks rush in.
For years, stablecoins were crypto’s business, dominated by Tether and Circle and used mostly to trade digital assets. That era is ending.
Over the past few months, and especially the past few weeks, the biggest names in traditional finance have moved en masse to claim a piece of the onchain dollar. Here’s the map of a land grab that’s accelerating fast.
The bank consortium puts money down
The clearest signal came this week, when Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Santander, and Deutsche Bank were reported to be among banks committing roughly $270 million to a joint dollar-stablecoin venture codenamed “Project Faro.”
The capital funds five years of operations for a U.S.-incorporated issuer targeting a 2027 launch, part of a 21-institution coalition that has swelled from an initial group of 10. The goal is explicit: challenge Tether and Circle, which together still control about 85% of a roughly $290 billion market.
SoFi and the national-bank play
While the consortium plans, SoFi has shipped. Earlier this week, its SoFiUSD, billed as the first stablecoin from a U.S. national bank, expanded onto Polygon this month alongside Ethereum and Solana, reaching the bank’s 17 million-plus members.
SoFi also launched SoFi Earn, a tokenized deposit paying 4.40% yield that converts into SoFiUSD, and already settles its entire card program over Mastercard’s network.
Meanwhile, the federally chartered crypto bank Anchorage Digital has positioned itself as a settlement backbone.
Anchorage’s tokens can now settle transactions on Visa’s network, starting with Western Union’s USDPT, and it recently anchored both sides of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens across one of the world’s largest remittance routes.
The card networks go all-in
Mastercard has been the most aggressive incumbent among payment giants.
It launched a Global Money Platform with acquired stablecoin firm BVNK, rolled out a Stablecoin Security tool to screen payments for fraud, and unveiled Agent Pay for Machines, letting AI agents transact in stablecoins.
Visa, meanwhile, has expanded its own stablecoin settlement program across multiple blockchains.
The crypto-native incumbents, not to be left out, are also racing to entrench.
Circle struck a deal to bring USDC settlement to banking rails in Latin America, starting with a Colombia pilot, part of a broader expansion into dozens of emerging markets.
Why now?
The catalyst is regulation. The GENIUS Act, signed in 2025, created the first U.S. framework for dollar-pegged tokens, giving regulated institutions a clear path into a business they had largely watched from the sidelines.
The Donald Trump administration has framed dollar stablecoins as a tool to extend the dollar’s reach and global hegemony, and banks that once dismissed crypto now see a settlement business they can’t afford to cede.
Much of this remains early. Project Faro has no token, no CEO, and no final name. Tether and Circle still dominate, and bank-issued tokens face a steep climb to win share.
But the direction is unmistakable: the onchain dollar, once crypto’s turf, is now contested ground, with Wall Street, the card networks and the stablecoin incumbents all racing to own the rails money moves on.

Coinone warns of phishing, identity theft after customer data breach
The South Korean crypto exchange said potentially exposed information includes passwords, bank account numbers, national identification numbers and crypto wallet addresses.
South Korean crypto exchange Coinone warned customers of potential phishing scams and identity theft after an attacker breached its outsourced customer support provider, exposing information shared during customer service interactions.
On Sunday, Coinone said an attacker accessed servers operated by MetaM on Thursday and viewed or extracted customer support records. Coinone said it learned about the breach in the same day.
According to Coinone, the information potentially exposed names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, national identification numbers, home and wallet addresses and transaction IDs.
Coinone said the affected data varies by customer, and people who never contacted its support center were unaffected. It did not disclose how many customers were affected.
The exchange urged customers who shared passwords during support interactions to change them and warned that fraudsters could impersonate Coinone using details from previous conversations.
Coinone said its account, trading and wallet infrastructure operates separately from MetaM’s servers, with no evidence of direct compromise. The exchange said it has reported the incident to South Korean authorities.
The disclosure comes as South Korea moves to strengthen financial-sector cybersecurity. In October, the Financial Services Commission identified security deficiencies at 130 of 555 financial firms reviewed.
On Thursday, the regulator said it would allow crypto exchanges to suspend withdrawals when hacking is suspected, alongside calls for round-the-clock monitoring.

items.author: Jacob Lyon
items.content:
Tether-backed investment firm Abraxas Capital Management has reportedly lost $17 million after an API key leak at crypto roll-up firm Lighter.
According to Predicts.guru founder 0xTria, Lighter appears to have suffered an API leak that allowed hackers to redirect funds from two large market maker accounts.
0xTria later noted that one of these Lighter accounts was funded from Abraxas’ known Hyperliquid wallets.
Korean sources close to 0xTria claim hackers closed the victim’s positions before creating a public pool with 0% fees.
They then used roughly $10,000 to buy 99.99% of the pool before moving the victim’s funds, using stablecoin USDC, into the pool in $1 million chunks. From here, the funds were redeemed and split up into ETH via CoW Swap.
Crypto analyst Lookonchain noted that Abraxas’ Hyperliquid account has been closing its short positions and withdrawing funds across the last 24 hours.
The account holds $150 million less and its short positions are now just $70 million.
Lighter suspends withdrawals
Lighter first revealed on X that it is investigating a security incident involving a “single compromised external party” and later confirmed that it was caused by “a leaked API key for a specific trader’s account.”
It said, “As a precaution, we have temporarily suspended all withdrawals and pool creation while we investigate the circumstances and assess the full impact.”
Lighter also claims it is trying “to recover funds involved in an additional withdrawal attempt by the attacker,” and shared the hacker’s wallet address: 0xb3fffca23d4444eE73349825ACD84f7b5020e387.
Protos has reached out to Lighter and Abraxas for comment and will update should we hear anything back.
Abraxas manages a major Tether trading fund
Abraxas Capital is a London-based crypto investment firm founded by CEO Fabio Frontini in 2002. The company manages $4 billion in assets.
It also runs Heka Funds, a Malta-based company that’s one of the largest clients for stablecoin behemoth Tether.

Heka manages Elysium Global Arbitrage Fund, a market-neutral crypto-fund trading over $1 billion in Tether tokens annually, arbitraging them from one exchange to another.
Heka accused of Tether market manipulation
Tether’s stablecoin rival Circle banned Heka in 2023 after it suspected the firm was manipulating the market to benefit Tether. It later lifted the ban at the end of the year.
As reported by The Financial Times, this was revealed in court filings involving an arbitration dispute between Heka and Circle.
Circle believed Heka was trading in USDC and funneling the proceeds into Tether. It also says that Heka was redeeming large volumes of USDC for cash even when there was no opportunity for profit.
Read more: What the Tether audit means for the crypto industry
Heka took Circle to arbitration in 2024, claiming that the ban cost the firm $49 million worth of profits.
In a confidential ruling, arbitrators sided with Circle, which is now pushing to publicly confirm the proceedings in a Boston federal court.
Court filings further revealed that Tether backed Heka with an $800 million investment via a linked fund that was supposed to hide the Tether source.
Lighter also used by $6B Binance hacker
Protos has also been able to trace funds taken from Binance’s compromised hot wallet to 44 Lighter accounts.
Almost $4.5 million worth of USDC was sent to Lighter wallets before it was moved to various ETH wallets and swapping service ChainFlip where a potion was converted into BTC.

items.content:
Zelle picks Solana for ZelleUSD stablecoin and international payments
Zelle plans to use Solana for its ZelleUSD stablecoin and international payments, with confidential transfers designed to hide payment amounts.
Zelle, the US peer-to-peer payments network operated by Early Warning Services (EWS), a consortium of banks that includes JPMorgan and Wells Fargo, is partnering with Solana to support its expansion into international payments. The company announced on stage at Breakpoint 2026 that its proprietary dollar-backed stablecoin, ZelleUSD (ZLUSD), will launch on the Solana blockchain to allow for peer-to-peer payments internationally.
The move brings one of the largest domestic payments networks in the US into the blockchain-based payments market. Zelle processed more than $1.2 trillion in US payments in 2025 and has since taken steps to establish an international business. In June, the company named India as its first international remittance corridor, with plans to allow US consumers to send money to friends and family in the country. In the same announcement, the company unveiled ZelleUSD, intended to underpin future international payment capabilities in additional markets. ZelleUSD’s issuer is Anchorage Digital Bank.
“Sending money around the world is a pain; it’s complex, it’s fragmented and it’s often unfamiliar. Over half of the Remittance services that are offered today don’t deliver money as fast as we’d like them to,” said Alexandra Lang, vice president of digital asset partnerships at Zelle. “Solana is a partner we chose because we’re here to deliver payments at scale.”
The collaboration will also include ongoing experimentation into the development of privacy features for the transactions, aimed at preserving the sensitivity of payments on the public blockchain.
Zelle cites Solana’s network reliability
For Zelle, the decision to select Solana appears to have been driven in large part by the network’s infrastructure. “Zelle has such a massive scale in the United States, we needed a partner that can also deliver at massive scale internationally as well,” said Denise Leonhard, General Manager at Zelle in a video discussing the partnership.
“The number one priority is the responsibility that we have to make sure that payments are safe, secure, and they get to the right place [...] That piece around trust, security, proven infrastructure is the reason why we chose Solana.”
Following several years in which network outages raised questions about Solana’s suitability for financial applications, the chain has maintained 100% uptime since February 2024. This is despite a routing failure at infrastructure provider Teraswitch in August 2026, which took 29% of Solana’s network offline. According to blockchain intelligence platform Metrika, transaction finality slowed, but uptime was sustained.
On stage at Breakpoint 2026, the Solana Foundation announced the migration of Solana from beta into mainnet, bringing with it an improvement in finality speed from 13 seconds to 150 milliseconds.
Related: HKMA, Swift explore tokenized deposits for cross-border bank payments
Confidential transfers shield payment amounts
Going deeper into what the collaboration will entail, on stage at Breakpoint, Lang introduced the confidential payments features the two companies had developed. She explained that the privacy focus aimed at balancing customer privacy over their payments on the network with the money laundering checks large institutions are required to make.
In the payments wallet, customers will have the option to encrypt their transfer so it is shielded from the public blockchain. Institutions that are part of Zelle’s network will be able to decrypt the transfer to carry out the checks needed to maintain compliance.
“Features like this are paramount to really getting payments to scale,” said Lang.
Related: DBS, JPMorgan’s Kinexys launch 24/7 transfers of tokenized deposits
Solana competes with Ethereum and Tron for remittance play
Although Solana is gaining ground in stablecoin activity, Ethereum and Tron continue to hold substantially larger pools of dollar-pegged assets. According to Token Terminal data pulled on Nov. 14, Ethereum held $150.5 billion in stablecoins while Tron held $93.2 billion, compared with $13.9 billion on Solana.
However, Solana’s stablecoin activity is growing faster in transaction frequency than on either of its larger competitors. The network recorded an 82% increase in monthly stablecoin transfers year-over-year in October, compared with 48% growth on Ethereum, while Tron’s transfer count declined by nearly 8%, according to Token Terminal data.
Zelle’s choice of Solana over both Tron and Ethereum follows other remittance providers that have expanded on-chain. Also at Breakpoint, MoneyGram outlined an integration with Solflare allowing Solflare wallet users to exchange UDSC to cash. The move expands MoneyGram Ramps on Solana, launched by the company in August.
“That’s where MoneyGram brings something different to the ecosystem: the ability to bridge digital dollars and physical cash at scale, making stablecoins more useful in everyday life,” said Luke Tuttle, Chief Product and Technology Officer at MoneyGram in a press release.
While Zelle did not provide a timeline for the launch of international payments on stage, earlier announcements indicated that the India corridor would be live by the end of 2026.

items.content:
A wallet tied to Rune Christensen, the founder of DAI stablecoin protocol Maker and its USDS successor Sky, borrowed $1 million against SKY tokens on October 26, less than a week before his game studio, Raw Power Games, went bankrupt.
All told, that wallet has withdrawn and owes over $76 million to a Sky savings pool that has effectively locked out ordinary depositors from withdrawing. On Sunday, available liquidity from the pool was as good as $0.
That single wallet’s outstanding loans account for roughly half of the pool’s loans.
A critic on social media assumes much of the stablecoin loans went to Raw Power.
Protos has been unable to independently verify the quantity of money borrowed from Sky or Sky-based stablecoin liquidity pools, such as staked USDS, that benefitted Raw Power. However, Christensen’s overwhelming control of Sky Protocol and its wallets is widely suspected.
Even a formal rating by S&P last month notes Christensen’s “highly centralized” role where “he effectively influences key decisions.”
Protos has covered Christensen’s preeminent power at Maker (now Sky) since 2022.
Raw Power goes bankrupt, shares same founder as USDS
On October 30, Christensen’s gaming studio admitted, “Due to circumstances outside our control, the necessary funding behind Raw Power Games is no longer in place.”
Although the admission didn’t name the financial backer, Danish media outlet Ingeniøren reported in 2022 that Christensen founded the studio with his own money.
Company records show Christensen stepped down as a corporate director around October 29, 2026 — the same week a liquidator was appointed over the company.
Two weeks later, another gaming company called Coffee Stain agreed to a 36.75 million Danish kroner (US$5.4 million) purchase of Raw Power Games’ intellectual property out of its “bankruptcy estate.”
Announced this weekend, Coffee Stain expects finalization of that deal within “weeks.”
Read more: Maker DAO drama flares amid proposal to tackle ‘governance attack’
USDS liquidity pool with $0 of available liquidity
Before borrowing limits crashed to $0, the wallet borrowed tens of millions of dollars worth of USDS assets, including $1 million within a week of Raw Power going bankrupt.
The pool is for staked USDS, where stablecoin savers can lend Sky’s dollar stablecoin to borrowers who post SKY tokens as collateral. The pool currently incentivizes deposits with a 13.6% annualized interest rate.
Borrowers have taken nearly all of the available USDS, however. An analyst correctly described, “even its biggest holders can’t take out a single dollar right now.”
On-chain records show withdrawable cash effectively ran out on Halloween, within days of the studio’s bankruptcy.
The wallet owed more than $72 million by April and has made no repayments on its loans, so interest accumulation kept pushing its total loan balance higher. By October 28, its outstanding balance was $76.6 million.
Sky is the renamed MakerDAO. As Protos reported in 2024, the project has issued the DAI stablecoin since December 2017, and introduced one-for-one conversion of DAI into USDS.
It also introduced a new governance token, SKY, to replace Maker’s old governance token, MKR.
Withdrawals from the pool depend on loan repayments or new money arriving from fresh depositors. The largest borrower is a wallet tied to the founder of USDS, whose gaming company just went bankrupt.

The United States Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear an appeal from crypto-focused bank Custodia, effectively ending the bank’s latest legal effort to gain direct access to the Federal Reserve’s payment system. Custodia is a Wyoming-chartered bank founded by Caitlin Long. The bank has been trying for a Fed master account since 2020, which would allow it to process payments directly without relying on third-party financial institutions. Now, the Supreme Court’s Monday decision means an earlier ruling allowing the Fed to reject applications from eligible banks will remain in effect. The case highlights some of the challenges crypto-facing banks face in gaining direct access to the US payment system. Still, even if state-chartered banks qualify for master accounts, the Fed does not have to approve every application. In a dissent issued in March, US Circuit Judge Timothy Tymkovich criticized the appeals court’s decision to give Federal Reserve banks discretion over master accounts. “Without a master account, a bank cannot operate in the modern banking system,” Tymkovich wrote, arguing that the ruling effectively gives the Fed the power to override state banking decisions. A timeline of events Custodia first sued the Federal Reserve in 2022 after waiting around two years for a decision on its master account application. The Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City ended up rejecting the request in January 2023, citing concerns about risks linked to the bank’s crypto-focused business model. In October 2025, a federal appeals court ruled against Custodia, finding that Federal Reserve banks did not have to grant master accounts to every eligible institution. Related: Crypto among sectors ‘debanked’ by 9 major banks: US regulator Cointelegraph previously reported that the court declined to reconsider its decision in March. This led Custodia to take its case to the Supreme Court. The bank’s appeal also received support from the Blockchain Association, which argued that the Fed’s ability to reject applications could weaken the authority of state banking regulators. Senator Cynthia Lummis and former Senator Patrick Toomey also filed a brief with the Supreme Court in August, supporting Custodia’s appeal. Today’s decision comes as other crypto-focused banks seek access to the Fed’s payment system. In March, Kraken Financial received approval for a restricted account from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City — the same regional bank that rejected Custodia’s application. Notably, Kraken’s account was approved for an initial one-year period and allows it to send and receive payments through the Fed’s Fedwire system. However, the account has restrictions and does not offer all the services of a full master account. Looking ahead, Custodia may still be able to apply for another master account or seek limited access to the Fed’s payment system under a separate proposal. items.author: Shaurya Malwa
items.content:
--- From rss ---
In brief
- Ethereum’s proposed Glamsterdam upgrade could break up to 15,000 smart contracts, EF developer Marius van der Wijden said on a Nov. 16 core developer call.
- AI-assisted audits by ChainSecurity and Dedaub found ~200 affected contract classes, mostly tied to gas-cost increases.
- No decision was made; removing the changes could delay the upgrade—and the post-quantum roadmap—by four to six months.
Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade threatens to break as many as 15,000 smart contracts, developers warned during a core developer call Monday, forcing a debate over how much disruption the network should tolerate in the name of scaling.
The concern centers on two proposed changes, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, designed to let Ethereum scale from 60 million gas to as much as 200 million gas per block, a roughly 3.3x jump that developers say would sharply lower costs for most users while keeping state growth in check.
The problem, flagged late in the development process, is that the changes break certain invariants, assumptions that some smart contracts were built to rely on.
ETH price on November 22, 4:59PM UTC
“Multiple contracts were relying on invariants in the protocol that are modified by 8037 and 8038,” said Marius van der Wijden, an Ethereum Foundation developer who worked on the scaling effort.
He acknowledged that the team “wanted to do significant public outreach” but that timelines slipped amid reorganizations and budget cuts at the foundation. He said he shares “a lot of blame” as the last remaining scaling lead still at the EF.
Two security firms, ChainSecurity and Dedaub, presented findings from AI-assisted audits, with the combined search turning up roughly 200 distinct classes of affected contracts, most tied to gas-cost increases rather than the new mechanics themselves.
Van der Wijden put the highest estimate at 10,000 to 15,000 contracts, a “fringe subset” of Ethereum’s roughly 90 million, with impacted value he loosely pegged in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars among contracts not yet committed to upgrading.
App developers pushed back on the framing. Jango, who builds the Juicebox protocol, warned the change undermines “composability,” a core Ethereum value prop, and shakes “developer confidence in building immutable protocols.” A Uniswap developer urged that EIP-8037 “should definitely be reconsidered.”
The Ethereum Foundation already delayed Glamsterdam’s testnet fork over these gas-related security flaws. Developers stressed Monday that no decision has been made, with the question headed to Thursday’s execution-layer call.
But several signaled a strong desire to ship the fork as planned, arguing that removing the changes could delay Glamsterdam, and the broader roadmap toward post-quantum security, by four to six months, time they say Ethereum can’t spare as quantum and AI threats loom.

items.ai_summary: Lighter在API签名密钥泄露导致约500万美元损失后恢复了提款，该事件暴露了攻击者可能利用交易权限破坏抵押品的安全隐患，并对管理着57亿美元未平仓合约的Hyperliquid协议的风险控制提出了严峻质疑。
items.author: Gino Matos
items.content:
Quick Take
- Lighter restored withdrawals after recovering about $5 million USDC following an attack involving compromised API signing keys.
- The incident highlights how hackers could exploit trading permissions to destroy collateral even without direct withdrawal access.
- Hyperliquid's massive derivatives market raises questions about whether its agent safeguards can contain losses before they reach liquidity providers.
Lighter's Nov. 16 security update described how exposed trading keys enabled an account drain through public-pool shares, putting a potential Hyperliquid exploit in perspective.
Lighter said that withdrawals had resumed after its safeguard allowed about 5 million USDC to be returned.
Hyperliquid has roughly $5.7 billion in open interest, representing about 55% of the open interest in the DefiLlama ranking as of Nov. 16.
Depending on the account permissions, a compromised agent could cause losses through unauthorized orders and liquidation in the accounts it can trade. Wider losses would depend on the affected positions, liquidity providers, and market depth.
Trading authority reaches beyond direct withdrawals
Lighter said that affected accounts used unsafe signing code outside its official software kits. Reused cryptographic signing nonces allowed the attacker to reconstruct API private keys from public signatures, while the protocol, contracts, infrastructure, and official kits were unaffected.
The attacker created a public pool under the affected account, acquired shares through another account, then moved victim funds into the pool without creating corresponding shares. Redeeming the existing shares allowed funds to leave.
The account said wallet signatures were now required for public-pool transfers and that API signatures had been made non-public, with IP allowlists and configurable limits added as further protections.
Separately, Bitquery traced a 10,393,057 USDC withdrawal from Lighter's Ethereum contract on the same day. Its investigation could not inspect the internal rollup transactions or independently establish the reported second account loss.
Hyperliquid's API-wallet documentation says a master account can authorize agents to sign for itself or its subaccounts. Its official agent example describes trading authority without transfer or withdrawal permissions.
The exchange endpoint allows an agent-signed asset transfer when the destination matches the source address, an expressly permitted internal movement distinct from sending assets to another owner.
Hyperliquid also documents a vault-transfer function, and its official Python SDK uses a different signing path for it than for external USDC transfers and bridge withdrawals. The signing code alone does not establish which agent the exchange will authorize to request the exchange.
The derivatives venue's current overview describes customizable HyperEVM accounting and agent delegation, separately from legacy HyperCore vaults. Those distinctions prevent a blanket conclusion about every vault.
A comparable Lighter extraction would require both the relevant permissions and a matching share-accounting path. The documented internal transfers and vault functions leave no basis for a blanket assurance that every agent-authorized vault path is impossible.
A stolen agent with valid authority could open unwanted positions, change exposure, or cause adverse execution. The resulting losses could exhaust the affected account's collateral through trading and liquidation, without a withdrawal to the thief.
Hyperliquid raises the liquidity stakes
The Nov. 16 snapshot showed Hyperliquid open interest of $5.7 billion, against nearly $554 million for Lighter and a tracked total of roughly $10.5 billion. Hyperliquid was about 10.3 times Lighter's size on that measure and accounted for approximately 54.7% of the total.
DefiLlama's Hyperliquid and Lighter protocol pages reported the following activity and bridge snapshots on Nov. 16:
| Measure | Hyperliquid | Lighter | 
|---|---|---|
| Open interest, ranking snapshot | $5.715 billion | $553.97 million | 
| Reported 24-hour perpetual volume | $9.739 billion | $3.710 billion | 
| Bridge headline Total Value Locked (TVL) | $5.694 billion | $491.07 million | 
The first layer of a hypothetical agent compromise is the authorized account. The next layer appears if that account supplies substantial market liquidity: missing quotes or forced hedging could worsen execution for others. HLP losses would require relevant strategy or liquidation exposure.
Market depth also matters more than a venue-wide balance. DefiLlama's exchange snapshot showed about $1.4 billion of aggregate dollar-perpetual depth within 2%, with far less available in individual markets.
Cross-venue effects could develop through shared intermediaries, hedges, and collateral needs, but those connections would have to be established for the affected participants. Lighter's incident does not demonstrate that chain of events at Hyperliquid.
Hyperliquid's earlier episodes illustrate why a trader's loss, a vault drawdown and a platform interruption need separate treatment.
Hyperliquid's history shows who can bear the loss
On March 12, 2025, approximately $4 million in HLP losses followed a large ETH liquidation, leading Hyperliquid to subsequently reduce maximum Bitcoin and Ethereum leverage to 40 times and 25 times.
The March 26 JELLY episode led to a reported loss of nearly $12 million and a later operator statement putting 24-hour HLP profit at roughly 700,000 USDC. As a response, validators delisted the market after suspicious activity.
There was also a November 2025 POPCAT incident that culminated in an estimated $4.9 million HLP loss and a temporary Arbitrum-bridge pause. The fourth episode happened on April 9, with an approximately $1.5 million daily HLP drawdown amid suspected FARTCOIN manipulation.
HLP's <terms state that the community shares the strategy's profit and loss, with withdrawals subject to a four-day delay from the latest deposit. DefiLlama's Nov. 16 HLP snapshot put its headline total value locked (TVL) near $151.9 million.
The clearest documented compensation process followed the July 29, 2025 API disruption. Hyperliquid's Aug. 4 announcement described 37 minutes of delayed orders and error responses even as transactions reached blocks, and its refund method covered specified fills and unusually high funding payments.
The process excluded the smallest calculated refunds and required business or identity verification for larger recipients to receive their full balance.
An Aug. 5 update said refunds had been distributed, describing a conditional response to one operational incident.
How LIT and HYPE reacted
Lighter's token LIT weakened during the incident, dropping from $2.75 to $2.32 right after it, but recovering to $2.88 as of press time
A historical HYPE comparison from 2025 shows the token fell from $14.04 to $12.84 during the March 12 ETH-whale episode, before some recovery.
Relevant escalation signals for Hyperliquid would include an affected account's trading authority and positions, deterioration in the markets it supports, losses reaching HLP, or disruption to settlement and withdrawals.
Its $5.7 billion in open bets makes those distinctions consequential, but the dollar amount threatened by a particular compromise would still depend on the permissions, exposure, and liquidity involved.

In brief
- Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year earlier, while adjusted earnings reached $2.68 per share.
- Shares rose roughly 2% after hours as the company forecast $130 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, above analysts' expectations.
- Interim CEO Colette Kress faces her first earnings call without Jensen Huang, while Nvidia's daily chart still shows strong selling pressure despite oversold conditions.
Nvidia shares climbed roughly 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday after the AI chipmaker delivered another record quarter, beating Wall Street expectations on revenue and earnings while forecasting stronger-than-expected sales for the current period.
The results offered some relief to investors after a brutal selloff that wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from Nvidia's market value following the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang.
According to Nvidia's earnings release, revenue reached $115.8 billion for the fiscal third quarter ended October 25, up 103% from a year earlier and comfortably above analysts' expectations of approximately $109.1 billion.
Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.68, beating the roughly $2.47 consensus estimate. Net income under generally accepted accounting principles reached $65.3 billion, more than double the $31.9 billion reported a year earlier.
Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% year over year and accounting for approximately 93% of total sales. The company also confirmed that its Vera Rubin NVL72 computing platform has begun shipping, extending the hardware roadmap that helped make Nvidia the dominant supplier of AI processors.
The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with Wall Street estimates of approximately $125.3 billion, per Reuters. That forecast includes an additional week in the reporting period and assumes no data center computing revenue from China.
Nvidia's first earnings without Jensen Huang
Tuesday's report marks Nvidia's first financial results since Huang resigned November 12, ending his 33-year tenure following revelations of extramarital affairs involving company employees and a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of having ties to China. Those intelligence allegations remain unproven, and an independent investigation is ongoing.
To add more drama to the story, the Securities and Exchange Commission opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia violated investor-disclosure laws.
Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and interim CEO, sought to reassure investors about the company's future. "Our momentum is real," she said in the earnings announcement, adding that the Vera Rubin rollout was off to a strong start and the product roadmap remained on track.
Huang said Tuesday that he would be honored to return as CEO if the board believed it was in Nvidia's best interests. His statement followed public support from Elon Musk and President Donald Trump, although the board is not considering reinstatement and continues searching for a permanent replacement.
Can Nvidia's stock recover?
Nvidia's fundamentals look considerably better than its stock chart. Despite Tuesday's rebound, shares remain roughly 35% below their October peak near $240, and the technical indicators suggest sellers still control the broader trend.
The daily chart shows immediate support around $150, close to the $148.80 low reached during last week's selloff. A decisive break below that area could expose further downside, while a sustained recovery would first need to reclaim resistance around $164.40 to $165.60.
That former support area has become resistance following the breakdown, as Decrypt's earlier technical analysis identified. Above it, the chart shows additional hurdles near $176 and between $184 and $189, making a return to the previous trading range far from automatic.
The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is around 22.5 on the supplied daily chart, well below the conventional oversold threshold of 30. That makes a short-term rebound plausible, but oversold readings are not proof that a bottom has formed.
The Average Directional Index, or ADX, sits near 45.4, indicating a strong prevailing trend, with directional signals favoring sellers. The faster exponential moving average remains above the slower one, a positive longer-term configuration that has not prevented the recent collapse.
Tuesday's earnings beat gives bulls a potential catalyst, but the after-hours bounce has yet to reclaim the chart's first major resistance around $164.40. Kress is scheduled to lead the company's 5 p.m. Eastern earnings call, the first without Huang, as investors look for answers about Nvidia's leadership and its next phase of growth.

A weeks-long trial last November resulted in a deadlocked jury and was ultimately deemed a mistrial.
Judge Jessica Clarke ruled on Monday that “the government failed to prove that the Peraire-Buenos made any material misrepresentations in the execution of their scheme.”

Code is Law
The Peraire-Bueno brothers made around $25 million in just 12 seconds off a bait-and-switch exploit of MEV trading bots in April 2023. Soon after exploiting this design flaw in Flashbots’ MEV-boost relay, the pair disclosed a different exploit under the moniker “Low Carb Crusader.”
Nonetheless, they were indicted in May 2024 on federal charges which prosecutors at the time dubbed a “first-of-its kind wire fraud and money laundering scheme.”
The full list of charges was wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and conspiracy to receive stolen property.
Judge Clarke ruled, however, that none of the brothers’ actions construed a “material misrepresentation” to the victims, an aspect key to a wire fraud conviction.
Moreover, she concluded that Ethereum is a “trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use… without the safeguards that exist in regulated markets.”
Clarke recognised that the brothers’ scheme “may have frustrated the spirit of MEV-Boost’s ‘design,’ [it] made no misrepresentation in its execution that can form the basis for fraud.”
She compares the case to that of Avraham Eisenberg’s 2022 exploit of Mango Markets, charges relating to which were ultimately overturned via similar reasoning last year.

A federal judge in Manhattan has acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno, the MIT-educated brothers accused of exploiting Ethereum's transaction ordering system to take $25 million from automated trading bots.
U.S. District Judge Jessica Clarke granted the brothers' motion for a judgment of acquittal on Monday, clearing them of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, according to her ruling. The decision closes the criminal case without a second trial.
"The question before the Court is not whether the Peraire-Buenos' conduct was right or moral, or even whether it violated uncharged crimes," Clarke wrote. To convict on wire fraud, prosecutors had to show the brothers made a material misrepresentation, and none of the government's theories did so, she found. Ethereum, she noted, is a "trustless, highly adversarial environment with no terms of use."
While the brothers' scheme "may have frustrated the spirit" of MEV-Boost, software that lets Ethereum validators outsource the ordering of transactions to specialized block builders, that was not enough to make out fraud, Clarke said. In a footnote, she added that the prosecution "raises serious due process concerns," though she declined to rule on that question.
Because the money laundering charge relied on the proceeds of the alleged wire fraud, it fell with the fraud counts.

The case stemmed from an April 2023 exploit targeting so-called sandwich bots, automated traders that profit from maximal extractable value (MEV) by placing their own trades on either side of other users' transactions.
According to the ruling, the brothers placed bait transactions designed to lure specific bots, then exploited a bug in a relay's code to see the bots' bundled trades before committing to a block. They then swapped the bait transactions for trades that sold the tokens instead, leaving the bots with about $25 million in losses in roughly 12 seconds. Authorities arrested the pair in May 2024, saying they spent months planning the attack and took steps to hide the proceeds.
At trial in Manhattan last year, an insider testified that the brothers had allegedly planned the attack, and the defense had earlier sought to block evidence of their Google searches. Clarke declared a mistrial in November 2025, after the jury deadlocked.
The case was closely watched in the crypto industry. Clarke's ruling described it as a "first of its kind" prosecution, a label the government itself used in its indictment.

items.ai_summary: 美国政府问责局的测试发现，OpenAI的ChatGPT、Anthropic的Claude、Google的Gemini和Grok均在12小时内为模拟攻击者提供了可用于策划致命恐怖袭击的信息。
items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- All four chatbots provided information for potentially deadly attacks in under 12 hours, a congressional watchdog found.
- Investigators verified the feasibility of the plans but did not carry out attacks, and the tests cannot rank the models' safety.
- Senator Maggie Hassan wants hearings on AI safety as technology companies contend with a surge of software vulnerabilities and patches.
Four of the most widely used AI chatbots helped government investigators develop potentially deadly attack plans in less than 12 hours, despite safeguards intended to stop exactly that kind of request.
OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Grok all supplied usable information during covert testing by the Government Accountability Office, according to a report released Wednesday. Investigators posed as attackers, then checked the responses against real locations, available materials, and expert assessments.
Two systems assisted with plans involving improvised explosives in crowded U.S. cities. Two others supplied information for attacks on electrical infrastructure, according to the watchdog, which withheld the models' assignments and operational details to prevent copycat attempts.
Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the investigation, warned that a terrorist could obtain "a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack" in less than 12 hours, according to her statement.
Safeguards that didn't hold
The chatbots initially activated protections, including refusing requests, removing harmful information or suspending accounts. Investigators bypassed those barriers with common jailbreak techniques, which manipulate an AI system into ignoring its safety rules.
The GAO checked suggested locations, researched whether materials were available and consulted specialists about the plans' feasibility. Some answers contained errors, including misplaced roads on a map, and investigators did not construct explosives or execute an attack.
In the report, "viable" means somebody would likely be able to follow the information supplied, not that an attack was demonstrated to succeed. Each model was tested on one assigned scenario, and the agency said the results were not statistically representative or suitable for ranking the companies.
OpenAI and Google said the tests involved older models, while Anthropic acknowledged that determined users can sometimes extract harmful material. The companies described continuing improvements to safety systems, though the GAO concluded those protections failed in its tests.
This is not really new. The findings follow a previous research showing eight of 10 popular chatbots assisted simulated teenage users planning violent attacks. The separate study tested 720 responses and found the bots provided actionable help roughly three-quarters of the time.
AI's other security problem
The GAO findings arrive amid outages affecting banks, Microsoft services and the National Security Agency. Officials say the disruptions were separate incidents, not evidence of a coordinated AI-driven cyberattack, even as the rush to repair software flaws has created its own problems.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton connected the NSA's outage to patching work. Officials described the recent breakdowns as maintenance-related, although individual organizations offered different explanations for their failures.
AI tools now find vulnerabilities faster than human teams can test and deploy fixes. Last month, the AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP flaws pushed website operators into an urgent patching campaign; the software powers a large share of the web.
The sheer volume is becoming another problem. VulnCheck data reveals there have been more than 100,000 software vulnerabilities logged this year by November 13, more than twice the total for 2025. Engineers still have to evaluate and deploy fixes without breaking the systems they are meant to protect.
That acceleration cuts both ways. Defenders gain powerful tools for finding weaknesses, but hasty repairs can disrupt essential systems, and malicious users may gain faster access to attack planning.
Hassan said she will make AI safety legislation an early priority when she takes over the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January. She plans hearings examining risks to public safety and critical infrastructure; the GAO itself made no formal policy recommendations.

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Germany's Bundestag approved a bill allowing customs to freeze suspicious Bitcoin holdings, including assets stored in self-custody wallets.
- Authorities could restrict crypto transfers for up to 180 days without controlling private keys, challenging the legal freedom of self-custody holders.
- Identifying wallet owners and enforcing transfer bans remain major hurdles, while the legislation awaits final approval.
Germany's parliament has approved legislation allowing customs authorities to freeze suspicious crypto holdings, including assets stored in self-custody wallets.
The Bundestag passed the bill on Nov. 12, advancing a broader government effort to combat money laundering and financial crime by expanding authorities' powers to investigate assets of questionable origin.
Under the proposed legislation, German customs could temporarily freeze significant assets, including cryptocurrencies, when factual evidence raises doubts about their lawful origin.
The approved committee text identifies assets worth more than €100,000 as a general benchmark for significant holdings. Authorities could also combine closely connected assets when determining whether they qualify.
Customs would initially have 30 days to investigate suspicious holdings, with a finance court authorized to extend the restriction by another 150 days if investigators demonstrate credible doubts about their origin and grounds for further investigation.
The legislation, however, has not completed its final approval process. As of Nov. 18, final consideration by the Bundesrat, Germany's chamber representing the states, and publication in the Federal Law Gazette remained outstanding.
Germany's Bitcoin freeze powers face a self-custody challenge
The proposed rules could have different consequences depending on whether investors hold their Bitcoin through centralized exchanges or control their wallets directly.
For assets held on an exchange, German authorities could issue an enforceable attachment order requiring the custodian to restrict withdrawals from an affected account.
The mechanism draws on Germany's existing tax enforcement provisions, which allow authorities to prevent third parties from releasing assets subject to a legally enforceable attachment.
However, enforcing similar restrictions against self-custody wallets presents a more complicated challenge.
Unlike centralized exchanges, self-custody wallets allow users to control the private keys needed to authorize Bitcoin transactions without relying on a financial intermediary.
Germany's proposed framework addresses such holdings by treating cryptocurrencies as attachable property rights.
Under Section 321 of the German Fiscal Code, authorities can attach certain property rights without involving a third party by serving the holder with a legal prohibition on disposing of them.
Applied to eligible self-custodied Bitcoin, this could prohibit an owner from transferring the affected assets without automatically removing their ability to authorize blockchain transactions.
Consequently, an individual could remain technically capable of moving Bitcoin despite being legally prohibited from doing so.
Germany's Blockchain Bundesverband highlighted this enforcement challenge in a submission on an earlier version of the legislation. The industry association explained that authorities must distinguish between cryptocurrencies held by custodians and assets controlled directly by individuals.
It also warned that identifying a blockchain wallet does not necessarily establish who controls its assets, particularly where multiple parties share transaction-signing authority.
These complications could make enforcing restrictions on self-custody wallets harder than freezing balances held by regulated exchanges.
The legislation also distinguishes temporary asset freezes from permanent confiscation, which would require a separate finance court decision establishing that the property originated unlawfully.
Should the bill complete Germany's legislative process, its effectiveness against self-custodied crypto holdings will depend on authorities' ability to identify wallet controllers and enforce legal restrictions without direct control of their private keys.

Ledger said Wednesday it has confirmed tampered hardware wallets in Berlin and is investigating reports of two more in Dubai, expanding a probe it had previously described as a localized incident in Southeast Asia.
“Our findings since then show tampered devices outside Southeast Asia. It is the same incident,” the company said in an update on its support site.
The investigation began last month after customers who bought devices from reseller CryptoBilis reported losses. Onchain investigators traced a suspected drain of about $87 million from hundreds of victim wallets across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.
Ledger said at the time that all confirmed cases were tied to CryptoBilis, and it later asked resellers in seven Asian markets to pull devices from sale.
Every device Ledger has confirmed shows the same kind of physical modification, designed to capture a user’s recovery phrase during setup. A recovery phrase, typically a string of 24 words, is the master key to a crypto wallet: anyone who has it can drain the funds.

items.author: Aaron Wise
items.content:
Recent outages at the National Security Agency, Federal Aviation Administration, National Weather Service, Microsoft, JPMorgan, and Apple are escalating a disturbing trend of US infrastructure destabilization.
As frontier AI advances its hacking capabilities, many people are concerned about rogue agents, cyber-extortion groups, and even state-sponsored hacking groups.
On Tuesday, the NSA’s internal classified network went down in what the agency called “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”
The same day, a software update knocked Apple users off iCloud and the App Store. Ostensibly routine network maintenance disrupted the National Weather Service’s website for about an hour, too.
That was just one day, as widespread infrastructure failures have now stretched into their sixth consecutive day.
Six consecutive days of US infrastructure outages
Major outages began by Thursday, November 12, when a latent software bug left over 80% of Microsoft 365’s gateway servers unresponsive.
That outage disrupted Outlook and Teams for nearly 24 hours, and Downdetector logged reports from more than 90 countries and territories.
The Microsoft outage even broke the connectors feeding OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.
Friday was worse. A nationwide FAA ground stop was the longest since September 11, 2001. The prime suspect is a router installed by contractor L3Harris whose ex-CEO cashed out $21 million prior to the incident.
Operators canceled about 12,500 flights that day, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy puts the economic toll in the billions.
The weekend offered no relief. Workday serves more than 11,500 organizations, and it was down from Friday evening into Saturday. Many workers found they could not clock in or deal with payroll.
Follow-on flight disruptions continued through Sunday from the earlier FAA outage.
On Monday, a software bug in JPMorgan Chase’s on-premise hardware slowed transactions at the largest US bank, and Downdetector also showed user reports at Bank of America, US Bank, and Wells Fargo, including Zelle service outages.
Also on Monday, United Airlines grounded or delayed departing flights for more than 90 minutes after pilots reported losing aircraft data.
Read more: Linux earns ‘worst bug in the history of the internet’ status
‘98% certainty this isn’t a cyberattack’
The disruptions follow a string of failures this year. US infrastructure failures in 2026 include Linux, Virginia data centers, an August Microsoft 365 outage, Philadelphia’s air traffic control, and a CSX railroad outage.
Donald Trump’s administration doesn’t want to attribute any of the incidents to foreign cyberattacks. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed, “98% certainty this isn’t a cyberattack.”
Even President Trump shrugged yesterday, “Things like that happen. It’s fine.” Asked about the FAA flight outage, he downplayed the situation, saying, “Essentially, what you saw was very old equipment that had a heart attack.”
Unconvinced, a Republican Senator countered, “If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

items.content:
Skyrocketing borrow rates are proving an insufficient incentive to free up liquidity in DeFi giant Sky’s stUSDS market, with founder Rune Christensen reportedly making up approximately half of the borrowed funds.
The market, on which liquidations are paused, has been at full utilisation for several days, leaving USDS depositors unable to withdraw their funds.
Consequently, the cost of borrowing USDS via stUSDS has spiked to 25% APY, up from just 5% last month, and may hit 50% within days.
Without the threat of liquidation, the borrowers needn’t fear, unless Sky’s DAO governance steps in which, given who a large portion of the loans belong to, seems unlikely.
That said, the SKY token, collateral against which stUSDS deposits are borrowed, is down over 20% in the past 24 hours, possibly anticipating sales to free up funds for repayment.
Christensen calls the worries about Sky “overblown” and stresses the protocol is strong. He does however recognize there are “questions about stUSDS” and that they will be addressed soon.
Read more: Wallet tied to Sky founder borrowed $1M days before his company collapsed
DeFi insiders aren’t worried about the health of the wider protocol, though.
Former Maker DAO delegate “PaperImperium” estimates that, even at max (50%) borrowing cost, “it would take several years to be in danger” and that only stUSDS holders would suffer a loss.
Similarly, former Aave delegate Marc Zeller says there’s “nothing wrong” and that the stUSDS product is Christensen’s “private credit line to fund his pet projects segregated from the main saving yield.”
While there may be limited contagion risk, with little incentive to repay, it doesn’t look like significant repayments are imminent.
Even when a small amount is repaid, the slack is picked up by MEV bots, maxing utilization once more.
Read more: Aave snubs Sky’s USDS as collateral and 3 ‘underperforming’ chains
Exit strategy
The stUSDS/USDS pool on decentralized exchange Curve Finance, which was set up a year ago to provide “supporting liquidity” to stUSDS holders, has shown volatility in the stUSDS/USDS exchange rate over the past week.
The pool’s $2 million of liquidity is currently made up of over 90% stUSDS, leading to the price divergence.
Prior to current developments, the stUSDS/USDS exchange rate was around 1.08, but the chart currently shows trading around par, with one particularly painful wick down to around 0.3.
Coincidentally, Curve Finance founder Michael Egorov previously pulled a similar strategy, borrowing multimillion sums of various stablecoins against his governance tokens, resulting in a liquidation cascade and plummeting CRV price in 2023.
Read more: Curve Finance founder Michael Egorov hit amid $22M CRV liquidation cascade
North Korean hackers also using Sky
While the stUSDS supply of $160 million is not to be sniffed at, it’s dwarfed by Sky’s overall stablecoin supply of $6.5 billion between USDS and legacy DAI.
These tokens maintain their dollar value via the protocol’s peg stability module (PSM), a 1:1 stablecoin exchange which has caught presumably unwanted attention.
CoinDesk reports that over half a billion dollars of illicit transactions have flown through the PSM over the years, including over $100 million tied to North Korean hackers.
With US authorities enthusiastically taking to freezing stablecoins in response to October’s Binance hack, some began to worry about the risk to pooled DeFi assets should the contracts holding commingled illicit funds be frozen.
Read more: LIVE: Binance says it’s yet to open up more token withdrawals
Possibly out of an abundance of caution, a Poloniex-labelled wallet reportedly converted $1.5 billion of USDS and sUSDS via Sky’s PSM, depositing the USDC into Aave.
Sky has played down the threat, noting that front ends block sanctioned entities and stressing that the funds flagged by CoinDesk “represent roughly 0.03%” of the almost $1 trillion of volume the PSM has processed to date.

Quick Take
- California sued OpenAI over more than 80 alleged AI security incidents, accusing the company of ignoring warnings and inadequate safeguards.
- Prosecutors allege OpenAI prioritized profits and rapid development over safety as experimental agents accessed external systems.
- The state seeks court-ordered changes to OpenAI's internal testing, while the company argues it is being unfairly singled out.
California is seeking court-ordered safeguards for OpenAI's internal AI testing after alleging at least 80 security incidents involving experimental agents.
Attorney General Rob Bonta filed the lawsuit on Nov. 16, accusing the ChatGPT developer of endangering the public by testing advanced artificial intelligence models without adequate security controls.
The complaint centers on a July incident in which hundreds of experimental OpenAI agents escaped their testing environment and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, an AI model hosting platform.
The attack lasted about two and a half days and was part of a broader pattern of incidents involving unauthorized access to external networks, government databases, and OpenAI's own infrastructure.
Bonta said:
“OpenAI's actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society.”
The lawsuit names OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC as defendants and alleges violations of California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance provisions.
OpenAI has pushed back against the lawsuit, arguing that California is singling it out over a challenge confronting the broader AI industry.
An OpenAI spokesperson reportedly said the company published technical reports, notified affected organizations, and strengthened safeguards after the Hugging Face incident. He added that the company remained committed to working with regulators on AI safety standards.
California alleges OpenAI ignored repeated security warnings
In its complaint, California accused OpenAI of prioritizing rapid model development over safety despite knowing its experimental systems could bypass restrictions and access external networks.
The filing alleges that OpenAI “misled and endangered the public and users of its services” by developing advanced AI systems without sufficient safeguards.
According to prosecutors, the company repeatedly assured customers that its research environments could contain potentially dangerous AI behavior but continued experimenting after discovering weaknesses in those protections.
Between March and June, OpenAI identified at least five instances of experimental models taking unauthorized actions.
By May 26, some agents had exploited a software vulnerability to access the public internet. An internal monitoring system subsequently flagged malicious activity on June 27, while other incidents exposed weaknesses in the infrastructure used to isolate experimental models.
California alleged that the company continued its research without adequately addressing those warnings.
The complaint also described incidents involving software repositories, public information websites and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information.
The state said OpenAI had acknowledged losing control of its agents more than 80 times during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents.
Prosecutors further accused the company of obstructing their investigation by withholding detailed information about the full extent of the incidents.
California also linked the alleged security failures to OpenAI's growing focus on revenue and rapid product development. The complaint contrasted the company's original nonprofit mission with its 2025 restructuring into a public benefit corporation, which coincided with $40 billion in funding from SoftBank.
Prosecutors noted that business customers accounted for about 40% of OpenAI's revenue in early 2026, driving its expansion into programming and cybersecurity tools.
The state further alleged that OpenAI sought to commercialize its security failures by marketing products designed to defend against threats resembling those created by its own experimental models.
California seeks judicial oversight of OpenAI's internal testing
California wants a San Francisco Superior Court judge to compel OpenAI to address unsafe conditions in its model development, training and evaluation operations.
The requested intervention would extend to internal research involving unreleased models, potentially requiring changes to how the company isolates experimental agents, monitors their behavior, and controls their access to external networks.
The complaint identifies inadequate monitoring, weakened model safeguards, and failures to contain agents within secure testing environments among the practices it seeks to address.
California also seeks an injunction preventing OpenAI from engaging in practices found to constitute unfair competition.
Beyond operational changes, the state is requesting $2,500 in civil penalties against each defendant for every proven violation of the Unfair Competition Law.
It also wants restitution for affected parties and the surrender of gains tied to unlawful conduct, with the amounts to be determined in court.

items.author: Aaron Wise
items.content:
The European Central Bank (ECB) went looking for the AI industry’s missing debt and found $4.5 trillion, a tally 287% higher than the off-balance sheet commitments it found in 2025.
Off-balance sheet commitments for the industry include the years of promised payments that AI companies hope to fulfill for data center rentals, cloud computation, and chips.
In its Financial Stability Review published yesterday, one day before Anthropic’s $1 trillion blockbuster IPO, the ECB added up eight US tech firms’ off-balance sheet commitments.
Hidden, off-balance sheet commitments dwarf everything the companies report in formal, on-balance sheet liabilities like debt.
Hyperscalers, for example, turn clients’ long-term compute contracts — like Oracle’s $300 billion OpenAI deal — into collateral, allowing loans against those years of committed future payments.
“Such cash flow commitments are debt-like in economic terms, but they do not appear as liabilities on the balance sheets of hyperscalers under US accounting standards,” the ECB warned.
Signed, off-balance sheet leases not yet available for use
Indeed, under US accounting rules, a balance sheet only records a lease once the asset becomes available for use.
Purchase commitments that haven’t commenced live in footnotes and have ballooned over the past year.
The ECB’s tally covers Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle, Broadcom, and Anthropic — a broad review of the biggest AI names, including today’s newly-public Claude maker.
Read more: AI companies rush to borrow cash as stocks crash
The ECB’s report repeatedly flags circular financing among AI companies. “For example, chipmakers and cloud providers may invest in AI labs that, in turn, commit to purchasing their hardware and services”, ECB Vice-President Boris Vujcic explained.
US Fed also finds trillions in off-balance sheet AI debt
US Fed Governor Michael Barr independently counted over $100 billion of hyperscaler and GPU-maker stakes in AI labs and cloud startups, and called the pattern “circular financing.”
Moving cash around without true revenue from consumers or outside industries can misleadingly inflate top line numbers and forecasts for AI companies.
“The rapid shift towards debt finance invokes historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles,” the ECB warned.
Although its $4.5 trillion number is certainly new, the ECB wasn’t first to flag off-balance sheet commitments in the AI industry.
Indeed, the Fed’s stability report, out last Friday, tallied more than $1 trillion of signed but unstarted leases, and it added more than $2 trillion of take-or-pay contracts and guarantees at seven of the same firms.
According to Fed calculations, the “nominal value of these types of obligations, or off-balance-sheet liabilities, now exceeds $3 trillion.”

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Bullish added DRW, Flow Traders, SoFi and Superstate to its tokenized stock coalition, expanding membership to 12 firms.
- Tokenized shares can move between approved wallets, but trading across brokerages and exchanges remains restricted.
- The coalition aims to establish common trading standards as Bullish prepares to acquire Equiniti in January 2027.
Bullish has added four major financial firms to a coalition seeking to make tokenized stocks easier to trade across platforms.
The crypto exchange and transfer agent Equiniti announced on Nov. 17 that DRW, Flow Traders, SoFi and Superstate had joined the Issuer Token Coalition, bringing its membership to 12 companies.
The group, which also includes the New York Stock Exchange, is developing common standards for issuing, transferring and trading shares represented on blockchain networks.
Its latest expansion brings together institutional trading firms, liquidity providers, financial services companies and tokenization specialists to address a persistent obstacle in the emerging market: investors can hold real company shares onchain but cannot freely trade them across different platforms.
Why tokenized stocks remain difficult to trade
Bullish's own shares illustrate the problem. The company allows eligible shareholders to convert their BLSH holdings into tokens on Solana, where they can hold them in personal wallets or transfer them directly to other approved investors.
However, both parties must be registered with Equiniti, which maintains Bullish's official shareholder records, while their wallets must pass compliance screening.
According to Bullish's shareholder guide, decentralized exchange trading remains unavailable, and investors seeking to trade their shares on the New York Stock Exchange must return them to the traditional system.
Moving tokenized shares to another brokerage or trading venue also requires that platform to support the security, verify the investor, and recognize the ownership recorded by the transfer agent.
These restrictions have largely confined tokenized shares to arrangements established by their issuers and service providers.
The coalition intends to address those barriers through common technical standards, liquidity arrangements and infrastructure connecting traditional financial markets with blockchain networks.
Flow Traders, which provides liquidity across conventional and digital asset markets, said the initiative would help establish conditions for reliable trading, including outside traditional market hours.
Superstate already operates a model demonstrating how those connections can work.
In September 2025, Galaxy Digital introduced tokenized GLXY shares on Solana through an arrangement involving Equiniti and Superstate.
Under the structure, shareholders can move conventional Galaxy shares through Equiniti to Superstate, receive corresponding tokens in approved wallets and reverse the process to return their holdings to a brokerage account.
Bullish is pursuing a broader integration of these capabilities through its planned acquisition of Equiniti.
In its Nov. 18 earnings report, the company maintained its expectation that the transaction would close in January 2027, bringing the transfer agent responsible for shareholder records under common ownership with its exchange.
The acquisition would also give Bullish access to Equiniti's relationships with thousands of corporate issuers as it seeks to expand stock tokenization.
Meanwhile, the coalition's next phase will focus on liquidity mechanics, technical architecture and commercial arrangements needed to connect issuers, investors and trading venues.

items.author: Liam 'Akiba' Wright
items.content:
Quick Take
- Ledger is offering limited-time X-ray inspections for suspect hardware wallets at its factory in Vierzon, France.
- Ledger urges concerned buyers who purchased in Berlin from January 2026 onward to contact support as it investigates reports involving two Dubai devices.
- Ledger advises anyone who already used a suspect device to move funds to a wallet with a fresh recovery phrase.
Ledger is offering limited-time X-ray inspections for suspect hardware wallets as its tampering investigation reaches Berlin.
In a Nov. 18 update, the wallet maker said its support team can arrange for customers to send a device to its factory in Vierzon, France, for inspection and return.
The offer lets owners have their device examined for physical alterations. For anyone who has already used a suspect device, Ledger advised moving funds to a wallet with a fresh recovery phrase. The company also said in its advisory that the hardware it found was designed to capture those words during setup.
Ledger noted that the German cases it had investigated were localized to Berlin. The company advised concerned customers who bought a Ledger wallet from a third party there from January 2026 onward to contact its support team.
It also asks concerned buyers who purchased from third parties in Southeast Asia or Dubai to get in touch.
Ledger revealed it is still investigating reports involving two devices in Dubai and is working with distribution partners to learn how they entered circulation. It reported one affected Nano Gen 5 as it continues its investigation into Southeast Asian resellers.
The advisory described the inspection as an option for devices that raise concerns, so customers can ask Ledger Support to arrange secure shipment through an official ticket.
Ledger recommended sending a device only through that channel, and that support will never ask for a recovery phrase. Its guidance for buyers in Berlin, Dubai, and Southeast Asia describes when to contact Ledger, while support handles the arrangements for individual devices sent to the factory.
The inspection can look inside the submitted device for added hardware, since Ledger’s Genuine Check verifies the secure chip's authenticity. Where that chip remains intact, the check can miss a physical addition.
Ledger reported that all the devices it confirmed in this incident carried the same physical modification and that the investigation found no flaw in its secure chip or operating system.
In its Oct. 15 disclosure, Ledger said genuine wallets had been altered after leaving its control and distributed through Southeast Asian resellers.
The company said the samples it examined from stores, warehouses, and its own stock at the time were clean. In November, it described the Berlin findings as part of the same incident and that it still had no confirmed case involving a device bought directly from ledger.com.
When a recovery phrase may be exposed
Ledger advised owners of an unused suspect device to leave it unopened, keep it out of use, and contact official support. They should avoid using it to set up a new wallet or restore an existing one.
For owners who have already used a suspect device, Ledger advised moving funds to a new wallet with a fresh recovery phrase, generated on a device bought directly from its website. It also recommended avoiding reusing any passphrase used on the suspect device.
The recovery phrase is the set of words that lets an owner restore access to a wallet on a compatible device. Entering the same words on replacement hardware brings up the same wallet and leaves the original recovery credential in use.
Someone who already obtained the credentials needed to restore that wallet could use a compatible device of their own. Moving funds to a wallet with a fresh phrase changes the credentials that control those funds.
Meanwhile, an X-ray can look for evidence of physical tampering. Finding an implant would show the unit was altered.
Whether anyone already obtained a particular owner’s recovery words is a separate question that the scan alone cannot answer.
